Summarize features by polygon/cell ID

Source: R/assignment.R
summarize_by_cell.Rd

Aggregates an sf point dataset into one row per cell. By default computes counts and means, but the aggregation function is configurable. It also returns a pooled value for each cell, its mean pulled toward the mean of the cells around it (estimate = "pooled", the default; estimate = "mean" leaves it out), and can return a range for one further observation.

Usage

summarize_by_cell(
  assigned_points_sf,
  response_var = NULL,
  predictor_vars = NULL,
  id_col = "poly_id",
  agg_funs = list(mean = function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
  cells_sf = NULL,
  deff = 1,
  sac = NULL,
  deff_max_n = 500L,
  quiet = TRUE,
  conf_level = NULL,
  area = FALSE,
  estimate = c("pooled", "mean"),
  obs_level = NULL
)

Arguments

assigned_points_sf

An sf object with a cell identifier column.

response_var

Optional response column name for per-cell aggregation: a single character string. A name that is not a column, or a column that is not numeric, is skipped with a warning.

predictor_vars

Optional predictor column names for per-cell aggregation. Names that are not columns, and columns that are not numeric, are skipped with a warning.

id_col

Preferred name of the polygon/cell ID column.

agg_funs

Named list of aggregation functions. Default list(mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)). Additional common options: median, sum, sd. A single function (agg_funs = median) or a character vector of function names (c("median", "sum")) is also accepted. A single function is named after the expression passed: a name gives that name (median, or f for a variable f holding a function), stats::median gives median, and any other expression gives agg1; pass a named list to choose the name. Anything else falls back to the default mean with a warning. The functions receive each column with its infinite values already set to NA (see "Details"), so they need na.rm = TRUE as they do for missing values.

cells_sf

Optional polygon sf layer to join cell geometries onto the output. When supplied, the return value is an sf object with the polygon geometry from cells_sf, with one row per cell in cells_sf. Cells that no feature fell in are kept, with NA summaries. Duplicate ID values in cells_sf would multiply those rows, so they are reported with a warning. Its ID column is the first of id_col, "poly_id", "polygon_id", "id", "cell_id" and "grid_id" it carries, the list and order assign_features_to_polygons() reads the polygons' IDs from. A summarised ID that matches no cell is reported with a warning, since the join drops it with its points; a cells_sf with none of those columns, or one that is not an sf object, gives a warning and a plain data frame (an error with area = TRUE). When NULL (default), a plain data.frame/tibble is returned (previous behaviour).

deff

Design-effect adjustment for standard errors. One of:

1 (default)

No adjustment; the classic IID standard error sd / sqrt(n), which assumes the observations within a cell are independent. No "deff_applied" attribute is attached, so a result carrying none was computed this way.

"variogram"

Compute a per-cell design effect from a fitted variogram: for n points in a cell with correlation matrix R, the effective sample size of the mean is n^2 / sum(R), so deff = sum(R) / n. This generalises Kish (substituting a constant off-diagonal correlation recovers 1 + (n - 1) * rho exactly) but lets correlation decay with distance, which matters increasingly as cells get larger and Kish's single-rho assumption degrades. Supply the fit via sac, or it is estimated when response_var is given and 'gstat' is available. Exponential, spherical and Gaussian models are supported, with a nugget and with several structured components (each weighted by its partial sill) and with gstat's 2-D geometric anisotropy (vgm(..., anis = c(angle, ratio))), applied as gstat applies it. A request that cannot be met falls back to "kish", with a warning of class "spatialkit_deff_fallback" that gives the reason and the ICCs: a model of any other family (named in the warning), or no usable model (none supplied and none could be estimated, or a rejected fit that could not be replaced by an estimate). The standard errors, intervals and cell_weight are then Kish's, and the uncorrected ones only where Kish's own ICC is 0; the deff_method column says which on every row (see "Value"). The variogram route needs an identified range, which a layer does not always have, so read deff_method for the fallback. A model with no structured component (a pure nugget) implies that distinct observations are uncorrelated, so it is applied as a design effect of 1 in every cell, not treated as a fallback. That includes the model estimate_sac_range() returns when it finds no spatial structure (an NA range whose rejected_reason says so): the answer is then a design effect of 1, deff_method reads "variogram", and no fallback warning is raised. Points with empty geometry count towards their cells' values but not towards the correlation, with a warning.

"kish"

Estimate an intra-class correlation (ICC) for each summarised column from the grouped data using a one-way random-effects ANOVA decomposition (one ICC for the response and one for each predictor), then apply Kish's formula per cell: deff_i = 1 + (n_i - 1) * rho. The ICC is the ANOVA (method-of-moments) estimator with Donner's n0 for unequal cell sizes, not the REML estimate a mixed model returns: on a single unbalanced draw the two can differ by 0.1–0.2 (one check with cell sizes 3 to 77 and a true ICC of 0.5 gave 0.33 against REML's 0.51), while balanced designs agree to about 0.01. Neither is wrong, so do not read the difference as a defect. Each column's ICC is used for that column's SEs and for no other: the response's ICC is never applied to a predictor, nor one predictor's to another. It is the response's ICC that sets cell_weight whenever a response was given, and the first predictor's own ICC otherwise. Requires at least 2 cells with 2+ observations and at least 2 residual degrees of freedom (N - k >= 2); the ICC is taken as 0 (no correction for that column) otherwise, and likewise when the estimate itself comes out at or below 0. The "deff_applied" attribute is attached when any ICC is positive, so when all are 0 there is none.

A positive number

Applied as a uniform design effect to every cell, as sd * sqrt(deff / n), exactly sqrt(deff) times the naive SE. Use when you have an external estimate of the design effect. Anything that is not a single finite number >= 1 (including a value below 1, which would shrink the standard errors, and NA or Inf) is refused with a warning and replaced by 1.

sac

Optional sac_range object from estimate_sac_range(), used when deff = "variogram". Supplying one avoids re-fitting the variogram and lets you inspect the fit the design effect is based on. A sac_range whose fit was rejected (its value is NA and it carries a rejected_reason attribute) carries no usable correlation function, so it is set aside rather than correcting by a shape that was not trusted enough to report a range: the variogram is then estimated as if no sac had been given, with a plain warning saying so, or, where that is not possible, deff falls back to "kish" with the fallback warning, which names the rejection. The exception is a sac refused because no spatial structure was found, whose model is a pure nugget: it is used, and gives a design effect of 1. A sac with no variogram_model attribute – a plain number or a units object, say – is a range without a correlation function, and is set aside the same way. A sac fitted to residuals (attr(sac, "detrended") TRUE) is used as given, with a warning when it corrects response columns (see "Design effects and variable types").

deff_max_n

Cells with more than this many points are subsampled before forming the n x n correlation matrix used by deff = "variogram". Default 500. It must be a single number of at least 2 when deff = "variogram"; anything else is an error.

quiet

Logical; suppress this function's progress message()s. It does not silence R warnings, nor the package's console log echo (see spatialkit_quiet for that). Default TRUE, unlike the tessellation functions, whose default is FALSE.

conf_level

Optional confidence level in (0, 1), such as 0.95. When given, every numeric response and predictor column also gets ..neff_*, ..df_*, ..ci_lo_* and ..ci_hi_* (see "Confidence intervals"). Default NULL: no such columns.

area

Logical, default FALSE. With TRUE, and cells_sf supplied, the result gains cell_area (each cell's planar area in the squared units of cells_sf's CRS) and n_per_area (the count of rows in the cell over that area, a point density; a rate of anything else is that thing's agg_funs sum over cell_area). The request is refused with an error, not answered with a number, when the cells' CRS distorts areas across them by more than 1 percent, measured as the spread of planar-to-geodesic area ratios over the cells: a density is a comparison between cells and is meaningless where the map scale differs from one cell to the next. Inside a UTM zone the spread is under 0.3 percent and the request goes through; the conterminous United States forced into one zone (14 percent), or a few degrees of latitude in Web Mercator (4 percent at 48N), does not. ensure_projected() with purpose = "area" chooses an equal-area CRS for lon/lat input; build the cells in it. Lon/lat cells are measured geodesically instead: their cell_area is sf::st_area()'s area in square metres (on the sphere with s2, sf's default), not a planar area in squared degrees, and the distortion check passes by construction; with s2 switched off, sf needs the lwgeom package for that area and the request is refused without it. The measured spread is attached as attr(, "area_error").

estimate

Which value of a cell the frame reports: "pooled" (default) or "mean". With "mean" the frame is the one described above, the frame of earlier versions, whose default this was. With "pooled" every numeric response and predictor column also gets a pooled value, w * m + (1 - w) * t: the cell's own mean m and a target t, the mean of the rows of the 8 cells whose observations' centroids are nearest (all the other cells when there are fewer than 10; the polygons are not read). The own weight is w = tau2 / (tau2 + sigma2 / n), where n is the cell's count, sigma2 the spread of the observations about their cell's mean and tau2 the mean squared distance between a cell's level and its target. Each column is pooled on its own rows: those with a value, a cell and a location. agg_funs, deff, sac and conf_level do not enter the pooled columns, and every other column is computed as with "mean". Lon/lat coordinates, and coordinates without a CRS that look like degrees, are projected for the distances between centroids, as resolution_profile() projects them. The projection is chosen from every row of the layer, those without a value or a cell included, so on such input the rows a column does not use can still decide the CRS its distances are measured in; a layer projected beforehand is used in its own CRS. When the input carries the record of its cells' count (see "Value") and that record names a projected CRS, the one the profile worked in, the distances are measured in it, whatever CRS the layer is in. The value is matched as match.arg() matches a choice, so an abbreviation ("m") is accepted and NULL is the default. See "Pooled values" for what the pooled value estimates and what its numbers rest on, "Value" for the columns and the attributes, and "Conditions" for the warnings.

obs_level

Optional level in (0, 1), such as 0.90, of an interval for one further observation in a cell, located like the data. It needs estimate = "pooled": the interval is the pooled value plus the (1 - obs_level) / 2 and (1 + obs_level) / 2 quantiles of the leave-one-out residuals of the pooled values, so its two offsets are the same in every cell. It is a statement about observations on average, not about each cell. It is a separate argument from conf_level, whose interval is for a mean and is not a range for an observation. Any level strictly between 0 and 1 is computed the same way; only 0.90 has been checked (see "Intervals: which one answers which question"). Default NULL: no such interval.

Value

A tibble/data.frame (or sf if cells_sf given) with per-cell summaries: the ID column, n (rows in the cell), one column per agg_funs entry per variable, ..sd_* / ..se_* for every numeric response and predictor, ..neff_* / ..df_* / ..ci_lo_* / ..ci_hi_* for the same columns when conf_level is given, cell_weight, deff_applied and deff_method when a design effect was requested (any deff other than 1), and cell_area / n_per_area when area = TRUE. An input column also called n is not allowed to shadow the count.

deff_applied is TRUE on every row when a design-effect correction was applied (exactly when the "deff_applied" attribute below is attached; under "kish", when any standard-error column was corrected) and FALSE when the standard errors are the uncorrected ones: a refused deff, or "kish" ICCs of 0 for every column (and NA on a cells_sf row no point fell in). deff_method names the correction the standard errors carry, since their column names do not change with it: "variogram", "kish" or "fixed" when the one requested was applied, "none" when none was, and "kish (variogram fallback)" or "none (variogram fallback)" when a "variogram" request could not be met and Kish stood in for it (the second when Kish's ICCs were 0 too). So deff_applied is TRUE on a Kish fallback row: test deff_method == "variogram" to keep only rows the variogram corrected. Unlike the attribute, both columns survive rbind() and dplyr::bind_rows() of many results. A fallback is also signalled by a warning of class "spatialkit_deff_fallback" (a Kish ICC of 0 under a "kish" request is reported on attr(, "icc") instead), which tryCatch(spatialkit_deff_fallback = ) catches without matching the message. It is raised when the correction requested was not the one applied: a refused number (the standard errors are then the uncorrected ones) or a "variogram" request that fell back to Kish; the condition of the second carries requested and used.

When a correction was actually applied, an attribute "deff_applied" is attached recording it: method plus icc_resp/icc_pred and deff for "kish" (icc_pred is a vector named by predictor column, one ICC each; deff is the primary variable's per-cell design effect, all 1 when only a predictor's ICC was positive; requested and fallback_reason are added when a "variogram" request fell back to it), deff/deff_rows/rbar/crs/max_n for "variogram" (deff is the design effect at the primary variable's non-missing count per cell, deff_rows at the cell's row count, which is the vector the log line summarises as a median and a max), and deff alone for a fixed number. When cells_sf is supplied, every per-cell vector in that attribute (deff, deff_rows and rbar alike) is realigned to the joined row order, so deff[i] and rbar[i] still describe row i; cells with no observations carry NA. No attribute is attached when no correction was applied: deff = 1, or a deff = "kish" request (or Kish fallback) whose ICCs are all 0. A deff = "kish" request, and a "variogram" request that fell back to it, always records the ICCs it estimated on an attribute "icc" (resp, and pred, a vector named by predictor column; NA for a variable type with no numeric column), whether or not they were positive enough to apply, so a result with no "deff_applied" still says what the ICCs came out as.

The ID column keeps its input type when cells_sf's ID column and the summarised IDs already have the same class. When the classes differ, both are coerced to character in order to join (logged as a warning), and the returned ID column is therefore character. Whole numbers are written out in full for that ("100000", never "1e+05"), so an integer and a double ID of the same cell still match.

With estimate = "pooled", each numeric column v with its prefix (resp_ or pred_) gains ..pooled_<prefix><v> (the pooled value), ..pooled_w_<prefix><v> (the own weight, 0 to 1; it is not a regression weight) and ..pooled_target_<prefix><v> (the target), and with obs_level also ..obs_lo_<prefix><v> and ..obs_hi_<prefix><v>. They follow every column listed above and precede cell_area and n_per_area, the response's first, then each predictor's. A cell with no row that has a value, a cell and a location gets NA, never a value made from its neighbours. Two attributes are attached. attr(, "pooled"), of class "spatialkit_pooled", records what was fitted: toward, neighbours, crs (the CRS the centroid distances were measured in), obs_level, conf_level, intervals and columns, a list with one entry per pooled column holding column, role ("response" or "predictor"), n (rows used), cells, df (values beyond one per cell, which sigma2 rests on), neighbours (the cells in each target), sigma2, tau2, own_weight (the median weight), share_alone (the share of rows that are the only one in their cell), loo and loo_se (the leave-one-out mean squared error of the pooled value, and its standard error over rows), loo_one_cell (the same error with one mean for all rows), structured and structure_p (whether the cells predict a left-out observation better than one mean, and the p-value of the F test of the cell means against one mean, which has to be below 0.05 as well), offsets (the two offsets of the interval), repeated, skipped, constant and status. attr(, "intervals") is the same data frame as attr(, "pooled")$intervals: one row per family of interval columns in the frame, saying what it covers, what it is centred on, its level and its method. Away from the observations no interval here is calibrated.

Where the pooled columns of a column cannot be computed they are NA, with a warning of class "spatialkit_pool_unavailable" and not an error, and the plain columns are returned. "Conditions" lists that class and the other warnings of the pooled columns, with what each condition carries.

When assigned_points_sf carries attr(, "count_rule"), or cells_sf does (the assigned layer's is read first), the result carries that record with one more element, check, whatever estimate is. The record is the one select_resolution() wrote: rule, estimate (the cell value the count was chosen for), cells, obs_per_cell, response, scored (what the profile scored at the count: the rows, the cells that hold one, the leave-one-out error among them, and the centres the rows were given to), partition, crs and scored_cells. It has class "spatialkit_count_rule" and a print method. check$estimate is "match" or "mismatch": whether the summary reports the estimate the count was chosen for (NA for a count chosen for neither). A mismatch is a warning of class "spatialkit_estimate_mismatch" (fields chosen_for, reported, rule, cells), and the summary is returned as asked. check$cells is "match", "differ" or "not checked: <reason>": the response is fitted again on the rows and cells given, with the estimate the profile scored, and its scored rows, its occupied cells and its leave-one-out error are compared with the record's, the error to a relative tolerance of 1e-8. The first that differs is a warning of class "spatialkit_cells_differ" (fields what: "n", "cells" or "loo"; scored; found): rows were dropped or moved between cells, or the layer is another one. The same class with what = "record" (fields field, scored, found) is raised when the assigned layer and cells_sf carry different records, so the rows were assigned to other cells than the cells_sf given: the cells of another selection, or the scored cells of a selection beside other cells built from its count, such as a lattice sized by it. check$cells is then "differ", whatever the comparison of the rows finds. The comparison is not made, and check$cells says why, when the response is another column or was not summarised, the profile read the selection half (select_on = "split"), the cells are not the ones the profile scored (scored_cells is FALSE or NA), the profile scored no estimate, the input has no coordinates, the features are not points (see assign_features_to_polygons()), or the fit was stopped by the limit on an exact search without the 'FNN' package. Cells and rows without a record, such as polygons the caller brings, are not checked and raise neither warning.

A row that is the same distance from two centres lies on the boundary between their cells, which happens on gridded locations. resolution_profile() scores such a row in the cell of the lower-numbered centre, and assign_features_to_polygons(), on cells built from the centres the profile scored, gives a point on that boundary the same cell, measured in the CRS the record names, so the comparison reads "match" on gridded locations too. build_tessellation() draws those cells in the CRS the record names, whatever CRS the seeds arrive in, unless its crs names another projected CRS. Cells built in another projected CRS are the nearest-centre cells of that CRS, so a row near a boundary, on it or not, can sit in another cell than the profile put it in. So can a row joined in longitude and latitude (rows and cells both in degrees), and a row that reached the record's CRS by another transformation than the profile's, which can settle a tie the other way. The comparison then reports "differ", with what = "loo" when it finds the same rows in the same number of cells with another leave-one-out error. The summary's own numbers describe the cells as assigned.

The comparison uses the fit of the pooled columns when that is a fit of the estimate the profile scored, and fits the response once more otherwise. Without the 'FNN' package that fit compares every pair of cell centroids (pooled values) or, for each row alone in its cell, every other location (plain means), and above options(spatialkit.exact_pairs_max = ) pairs it is not made ("not checked: work limit"). A summary is not compared when neither layer carries the record: attr(x, "count_rule") <- NULL on the assigned layer and on cells_sf removes it.

Details

This is the third step of the package's pipeline, taking the labelled layer from assign_features_to_polygons() down to cell level. What distinguishes it from a plain dplyr::group_by() + summarise() is that it carries the uncertainty of each aggregate with it: alongside every mean it returns a within-cell standard deviation, a standard error and an observation count, and it can correct that standard error for within-cell spatial autocorrelation via deff. Reach for it whenever the cell-level values will be modelled or mapped, because a cell mean over 2 observations and one over 200 are not the same measurement and nothing downstream can tell them apart otherwise.

In addition to user-specified aggregation functions, this function always computes within-cell standard deviation (..sd_<var>) and standard error (..se_<var>) for every numeric response/predictor column, plus an n column (rows falling in the cell) and a cell_weight column. These columns let downstream models account for the fact that a cell with 2 observations carries more aggregation uncertainty than one with 200.

cell_weight is the effective sample size of the primary variable: the response when one was supplied, otherwise the first predictor. It counts that variable's non-missing rows, not all rows (a cell of 10 rows with 3 finite responses carries 3 observations' worth of information about the response, not 10), and it is divided by that cell's design effect when deff applied one. With deff = 1 and no missing values it equals n. Pass it as the weights argument of a downstream regression.

An infinite value (Inf, -Inf) in a response or predictor column is treated as missing, as NA and NaN are, in every statistic of that column: the agg_funs results, ..sd_*, ..se_*, the interval columns, ..neff_*, cell_weight and the design effect. n still counts the row. A warning of class "spatialkit_nonfinite" names the columns and gives the number of rows and cells affected (the condition carries n and columns). kriging_adequacy(), resolution_profile(), estimate_sac_range() and prep_model_data() leave such rows out too, so the steps of one pipeline agree on a cell's mean. A function in agg_funs therefore never sees an infinite value: max returns the largest finite value, and infinities cannot be counted through agg_funs.

Spatial autocorrelation and standard-error bias

By default (deff = 1), the ..se_* columns are computed as sd / sqrt(n), which treats the observations within each cell as independent. When data are spatially autocorrelated (the common case for the spatial workflows this package supports), within-cell observations are typically positively correlated: they share the cell's departure from the population mean, so as an estimate of the population (grand) mean a cell mean has an effective sample size smaller than n. For that estimand the naive SE is anticonservative (too small), and a downstream weighted regression that uses cell_weight or the ..se_* columns for population-level inference will produce overconfident standard errors for cells with strong intra-cell correlation. For the cell's own mean the naive SE is the right one when the cell's points are spread through it, and the corrected SE is too wide; see "What the standard error estimates" before setting deff.

Setting deff = "kish" applies an approximate correction using Kish's design effect. An intra-class correlation (ICC) is estimated for every summarised column on its own, the response and each predictor, via a one-way random-effects decomposition across all cells. Each column's ICC is used for that column's SE adjustment, and each cell's effective sample size is reduced to n_i / (1 + (n_i - 1) * rho). This is a first-order correction that does not require a full spatial covariance model but does require enough cells and observations for a stable ICC estimate.

A design effect estimated from the data ("kish" or "variogram") comes with a second, small-sample correction. The within-cell correlation that inflates the variance of the mean to sigma^2 * deff / n also biases the within-cell sample variance downward: under exchangeable correlation rho (Kish's own assumption), with deff = 1 + (n - 1) * rho, E[s^2] = sigma^2 * (n - deff) / (n - 1), so s^2 understates sigma^2 by very nearly the factor by which deff inflates the mean's variance, and the two errors compound rather than cancel. The standard error is therefore s * sqrt(deff / n) * sqrt((n - 1) / (n - deff)), and NA where deff >= n (the cell then holds one observation's worth of information and s carries none about sigma). This is the package's own derivation, not taken from a reference. Measured 95% interval coverage at n = 30 over 20,000 replicates: 0.921, 0.844 and 0.628 at rho = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 with s * sqrt(deff / n) alone, against 0.948, 0.950 and 0.949 with the rescaling.

You may also pass a fixed numeric design effect (e.g. deff = 2) to uniformly inflate standard errors: an externally supplied constant is applied as sd * sqrt(deff / n), exactly sqrt(deff) times the naive SE in every cell. (The E[s^2] correction that the estimated design effects also apply is derived from within-cell correlation and would not be justified for a number the caller chose.)

Even with the Kish correction, the adjusted SE is an approximation. For rigorous inference under spatial dependence, consider fitting an explicit spatial covariance model (e.g. via fit_bayesian_spatial_model).

What the standard error estimates

What the ..se_* columns estimate follows deff. At the default, deff = 1, sd / sqrt(n) is the standard error of the cell's own mean, the mean of the units the cell holds, and it is the right one when the cell's observations are spread through the cell. Under deff = "kish", "variogram" or a number other than 1 the columns are the standard error of the cell mean as an estimate of the population (grand) mean: the unconditional quantity, in which the cell's own realised deviation is part of the error, widened for the correlation inside the cell. That is the right quantity when cells are treated as samples from a common population: measured 95% interval coverage of the grand mean is 0.95 with deff = "kish" (and 0.29 with the naive SE) on exchangeable within-cell correlation, and 0.93 with deff = "variogram" on a simulated Gaussian field.

The corrected standard error is not that of the cell's own mean (the block average over that cell), which is what a cell-level map or a regression on cell values usually wants. For that quantity the naive sd / sqrt(n) is the better of the two on offer: measured coverage 0.95 under exchangeable within-cell correlation, against very nearly 1.00 for the design-effect-corrected SE, which is too wide by the factor sqrt(deff / (1 - rho)) (4.6 at 20 points a cell and rho = 0.5). That 0.95 is exact under the exchangeable model and holds under a spatial covariance model only when the cell's points are spread through the cell; with clustered sampling inside a cell it is anticonservative for the block average too (measured 0.58), and the right quantity there is a block-kriging variance, which this function does not compute. Use deff when the cell means feed a population-level inference; leave it at 1 when they are measurements of the cells themselves and the sampling within cells is reasonably uniform.

Design effects and variable types

deff = "kish" estimates a separate ICC for each summarised column, the response and every predictor, and applies each to that column alone: listing or removing a predictor leaves every other column's standard error, effective n and interval as they were. (One ICC used to be pooled over all the predictors, which was right for a column only when they all shared it: beside a predictor with an ICC of 0.87, one with an ICC of 0 had its standard error multiplied by 3.1.) deff = "variogram" fits or accepts one correlation function and applies it to every numeric column, because a variogram is a property of the field being modelled rather than of a variable type; a predictor whose spatial structure differs markedly from the response's will have its SE corrected by the response's correlation. The internally estimated variogram is fitted to the response itself, never to OLS residuals, whatever predictor_vars holds: the ..se_resp_* columns estimate the grand mean of the response, so the correlation to correct for is the response's own. (A residual variogram, whose correlation is that of the part the predictors do not explain, is weaker; using it here dropped grand-mean coverage from 0.93 to 0.51 the moment a predictor was listed.) Pass sac explicitly when you want a different variogram, such as a residual one from estimate_sac_range(..., predictor_vars = ). A sac whose attr(sac, "detrended") is TRUE is used as given, but when it corrects response columns a warning says that their standard errors are understated, as kriging_adequacy() warns about the same mismatch.

Confidence intervals

With conf_level set, every numeric response and predictor column gains four more columns: ..neff_*, that column's effective sample size in the cell (its non-missing count over its design effect, the per-column version of cell_weight); ..df_*, the degrees of freedom the interval uses; and ..ci_lo_* / ..ci_hi_*, a t interval for a mean. Which mean follows deff, as for ..se_*: at the default, deff = 1, the cell's own mean, when its observations are spread through the cell; under deff = "kish", "variogram" or a number other than 1, the cell mean as an estimate of the population (grand) mean. Everything in "What the standard error estimates" applies to it, including that the corrected interval is not one for the cell's own block average. The interval is mean +/- qt((1 + conf_level) / 2, df) * se, centred on the plain mean of the column's non-missing values whatever agg_funs computes, and is NA wherever the standard error is (a single observation; complete redundancy under deff). ..neff_* and ..df_* are NA where the column has one non-missing value or none, like the standard error; cell_weight still counts such a cell (1, or 1 / deff for a numeric deff), so the two differ there.

At no setting is ..ci_* a range for one observation: it is an interval for a mean, and it narrows as a cell's count grows where the spread of single observations does not. The interval for one further observation in a cell has its own argument and columns, obs_level with estimate = "pooled" and ..obs_lo_* / ..obs_hi_* (see "Intervals: which one answers which question"). In the simulation described there, ..ci_* at conf_level = 0.90 held 58.9 percent of the observations held out among the others, and the interval for one observation at obs_level = 0.90 held 89.6 percent. Away from the observations no interval here is calibrated.

The degrees of freedom are not neff - 1. The interval's spread comes from the within-cell sample variance, and under exchangeable correlation (deff = "kish") that variance keeps its n - 1 degrees of freedom whatever the design effect. The design effect inflates the mean's variance and biases s^2, both of which the standard error already corrects, and the resulting pivot is exactly t on n - 1 df. Measured 95% coverage of the grand mean on the Kish path, 20 cells of 20 at an ICC of 0.2 / 0.6 / 0.9: 0.954 / 0.953 / 0.952 with n - 1, against 0.992 / 1.000 / 1.000 with neff - 1, which is not an interval so much as a refusal to say anything. The effective-sample-size degrees of freedom of Faes et al. (2009) belong to a mean estimated across many correlated units whose variance is estimated from the spread between them; they do not transfer to a single cell's mean with a variance estimated from inside it. ..df_* is therefore n - 1 at deff = 1, for a numeric deff and for "kish". Under deff = "variogram" correlation decays with distance and the within-cell variance loses degrees of freedom to it; ..df_* is then the Satterthwaite (1946) moment-matched df of s^2 under the fitted correlation matrix, a fraction of n - 1 that shrinks as the range grows. Measured on a Gaussian field with an exponential range of 150 and 400 on a 1000-unit domain, 16 cells of about 25 points: 0.960 and 0.958 with that df, against 0.931 and 0.918 with n - 1, and 0.34 and 0.19 for the naive deff = 1 interval. The interval is only as good as the design effect under it: a mis-specified variogram, or an ICC estimated from too few cells, moves the coverage with it.

Pooled values

With estimate = "pooled" every numeric column also gets a pooled value. That is the default; estimate = "mean" leaves the pooled columns out and returns the frame of earlier versions. A cell's value, plain or pooled, estimates the cell's level: the expected value of one further observation located in the cell the way its observations were. It is not the average of a surface over the cell's area, which would give weight to ground that holds no observation.

For one column, write n, S and m = S / n for the count, the sum and the mean of a cell's rows, N for the rows in all and K for the cells that hold one. Then

  • sigma2 = sum((y - m)^2) / (N - K) is the spread of the observed values about their cell's mean;

  • the target t of a cell is the mean of the rows of its neighbours, sum(S) / sum(n) over them. The neighbours are the 8 cells whose centroids are nearest, the centroid of a cell being the mean of the coordinates of its rows. The polygons are not read, so two cells are neighbours whether or not they touch, and a cell is never its own neighbour;

  • tau2 = max(0, (sum(n * (m - t)^2) - K * sigma2) / N) is the mean squared distance between a cell's level and its target, the target's own error included;

  • the own weight is w = tau2 / (tau2 + sigma2 / n);

  • the pooled value is w * m + (1 - w) * t.

The own weight is the share of the pooled value that is the cell's own mean. It grows with the cell's count and with tau2. At 1 the pooled value is the plain mean; at 0 it is the target and holds none of the cell's own values. Pooled values are for maps and for predicting observations. ..pooled_w_* is not a regression weight. The plain columns are the same under either estimate, and they are the ones to use, with cell_weight, in a regression on cell values: each column is pulled toward its neighbours by its own amount, so a regression of pooled responses on pooled predictors is not a regression of the levels.

The cells can be any polygons the rows were assigned to, the package's own or ones the caller brings, with IDs of any type: only each row's cell and location are read. Each column is pooled on its own rows, those with a value, a cell and a location, with its own centroids, neighbours, sigma2 and tau2; a missing value in one column changes nothing in another. A cell with one such row gets a value. A cell with none gets NA, never a value made from its neighbours. The pooled columns do not read agg_funs or deff: the mean that is pooled is the arithmetic mean whatever agg_funs computes, and no design effect enters sigma2, tau2, the weights or the interval of obs_level.

Three cases change what the numbers rest on, and each is a warning (see "Conditions"). With 2 to 9 cells the neighbours of a cell are all the others, so its target is the mean of every row outside it, and the overall mean lies between that target and the cell's own mean. A cell whose own weight is below its share of the rows, n / N, then gets a pooled value on the far side of the overall mean from its plain mean, and two cells can change order. When few cells hold two rows, sigma2 is estimated from few values and every weight rests on it: df in attr(, "pooled") is the number of values beyond one per cell. And when tau2 comes out at 0, every own weight is 0 and each pooled value is its target; with two cells that is the other cell's mean, so the two values change places.

A tie between two candidate neighbours goes to the centroid with the lower x, then the lower y, and the centroids are summed with the rows in coordinate order, so a cell's neighbours do not depend on the order of the rows. The values then agree to rounding: a cell's sums are taken in the order of its rows. The tie is between distances computed from the coordinates in the CRS the distances are measured in (see estimate), so on gridded locations the same layer in another CRS or unit can give a cell another neighbour.

The figures on this page that describe pooled values and the two intervals come from one simulation, dev/sim-pooled-values.R in the package's repository, whose header holds its settings and seeds. It draws 200 layers on a square of side 1,000. Each has 2,100 clustered locations (four fifths of them round 25 parent points with a standard deviation of 40, the rest uniform) and a response that is a field with covariance exp(-d / 100) plus noise of variance 0.3. The 300 locations nearest a random centre are held out as a block, 300 of the others are held out at random, and the 1,500 left are the layer: 333 cells at 4.5 observations a cell from resolution_profile() with partition = "density", select_resolution(criterion = "size"), get_voronoi_seeds(), build_tessellation() and assign_features_to_polygons(), summarised with estimate = "pooled". A held-out observation is given the value of its cell by cell_values_at(). At the observations held out at random the root mean squared error of the pooled value was 0.96 of the plain mean's: 0.84 in cells that hold one of the layer's observations, 0.95 in cells of 2 to 4, 0.98 in cells of 5 to 9 and 0.99 in cells of 10 or more. In the held-out block it was 0.95.

structured in attr(, "pooled") says whether these cells predict a left-out observation better than one mean for all rows. It is FALSE when the leave-one-out error of one mean (loo_one_cell) is within 2 percent of that of the pooled values (loo) or below it, or when the F test of the cell means against one mean has p >= 0.05 (structure_p). FALSE raises a warning of class "spatialkit_no_structure", and the values are returned. On a response without spatial structure they still make a smooth map, because each is mostly the mean of its neighbours. With white noise as the response on the simulation's 200 layers the median own weight was 0.11, tau2 was 0 on 20 layers, the warning was raised on all 200, and a cell's pooled value had a correlation of 0.79 with the mean of the pooled values of its 8 nearest cells, where the plain means had one of -0.02.

The pooling model implies an error variance for a pooled value as an estimate of the cell's level, (1 - w) * tau2. It is not returned, and neither is an interval for the level, because no check has confirmed an interval built from it; sigma2, tau2 and ..pooled_w_* are in the result for a reader who wants to form it. In the simulation, with a cell's level taken as the mean of the noise-free field over further locations drawn in it like the data's, the squared error of the pooled value was 0.98 of (1 - w) * tau2 among the observations and 6.9 times it in the held-out block: away from the observations it is too small.

Beside a sharp boundary the pooled value can be further from a cell's level than the plain mean, because its target takes in cells across the boundary. A second simulation measured this on fields whose level jumps at county boundaries: one level for each county, alone and with a smooth field added, on two layouts of real locations (892 and 2,634 points, each in a county), with noise of 5, 20 or 50 percent of an observation's variance, 200 layers of each, five random folds, and on each fold the cells the package's defaults build from the training observations. A held-out observation is a boundary row when every training observation of its cell lies in its own county and more than half of those of the cell's neighbours lie in other counties. Boundary rows were 21.75 to 28.04 percent of the held-out observations. Over them the root mean squared error of the pooled value against the noise-free field, as a geometric mean over the layers of its ratio to the plain mean's, was from 9.16 percent lower to 56.36 percent higher. On county levels alone it was 43.21 and 56.36 percent higher with 5 percent noise, 11.23 and 20.58 percent higher with 20 percent, and from 3.79 percent lower to 1.47 percent higher with 50 percent; with the smooth field added it was from 9.16 percent lower to 1.59 percent higher. Over all held-out observations the pooled value's error was the lower of the two in every setting, by 1.75 to 18.73 percent.

Intervals: which one answers which question

Two families of interval columns can be in the frame. Each has its own argument, and neither changes the other.

FamilyColumnsTargetCentreAsked for by
observation..obs_lo_*, ..obs_hi_*one further observation in the cellpooled valueobs_level
mean..ci_lo_*, ..ci_hi_*a mean, never one observationplain meanconf_level

The observation of the first is one located in the cell the way the data's were. obs_level needs estimate = "pooled": without it the call is an error, not an interval round the plain mean. The mean the second covers follows deff: at deff = 1 the cell's own mean, when its observations are spread through the cell; under deff = "kish", "variogram" or a number other than 1 the cell mean as an estimate of the population mean (see "Confidence intervals", which also describes ..neff_* and ..df_*). No interval and no standard error is returned for a cell's level as the pooled value estimates it. attr(, "intervals") says the same of the frame in hand, one row per family present.

The interval for one observation is the pooled value plus two quantiles of the leave-one-out residuals of the pooled values. The residual e of a row is its value minus the pooled value of its cell computed without it: the cell's mean and own weight are computed again without the row, and sigma2, tau2 and the targets are held. With p = (1 - obs_level) / 2, ..obs_lo = pooled + quantile(e, p) and ..obs_hi = pooled + quantile(e, 1 - p).

  • It is a statement about observations on average: of further observations located like the data, about obs_level of them fall inside the interval of their cell. It does not hold cell by cell (the second simulation below gives the coverage in cells of one observation).

  • The two offsets are the same in every cell. The interval's centre varies over the map and its width does not. It does not narrow where a cell holds more rows: the offsets are quantiles of the errors of predicting single observations, and the spread of observations inside a cell is in every one of them.

  • It is wide. One observation is uncertain.

  • Only the level 0.90 has been checked. Another level is computed the same way.

  • Each residual is the error of predicting an observation from the other rows of its cell and from the cells around it, so the interval describes locations among the observations. A cell's value and interval describe the part of the cell where its observations lie, and a Voronoi cell can reach far past them toward the edge of the study area. The interval is too narrow for a cell with no observation, a gap in the layer or ground beyond the layer's edge.

In the simulation described under "Pooled values", the interval at obs_level = 0.90 held 89.6 percent of the observations held out at random among the others (83.7 to 94.0 percent in single layers) and 75.1 percent of those in the held-out block. ..ci_* at conf_level = 0.90, read as a range for one observation, held 58.9 and 49.2 percent of them, over the held-out observations whose cell has that interval. cell_values_at() returns each location's distance from the nearest observation, and its help gives the coverage by that distance.

The second simulation described under "Pooled values" read the interval at obs_level = 0.90 on smooth fields of two ranges and on county levels with a smooth field, with 20 or 50 percent noise, on both layouts: twelve settings. Setting by setting it held 89.38 to 89.79 percent of the held-out observations. Counted by the training observations in an observation's cell (1, 2 to 4, 5 to 9, 10 or more), it held at least 85.65 percent in every class but one: on county levels with a smooth field, on the layout of 892 points with 20 percent noise, it held 83.74 percent of the 4,878 observations whose cell held one training observation. On fields of that kind it is not a 90 percent interval in such cells: there it held 83.74 to 87.83 percent with 20 or 50 percent noise, and 82.64 and 82.94 percent with 5 percent.

Away from the observations no interval here is calibrated.

Conditions

What the pooled columns and the count record have to say is raised as R warnings with a class, so tryCatch(<class> = ) and withCallingHandlers() catch each without matching its text. A warning of the pooled columns is raised once per call and reason, for all the columns it applies to: its text names them and the condition carries them in columns, in the order of the pooled columns. A field said to be by column is a vector named by those columns, and the numbers of each column are in attr(, "pooled").

  • "spatialkit_pool_unavailable": the pooled columns of a column are NA. The plain columns are returned, and this is never an error. reason is "no coordinates" (a layer without geometry), "no located value" (no row with a value, a cell and a location), "no cell holds two values" (the condition also carries n and cells by column) or "work limit". The last is the case of many cells without the 'FNN' package: the neighbour search then compares every pair of cells and is not made above getOption("spatialkit.exact_pairs_max", 2e9) pairs, which is about 44,700 cells (the condition also carries work, limit, and cells by column). With 'FNN' there is no such limit, and the result is the same.

  • "spatialkit_pool_degenerate": the pooled values were computed and carry no pooling. reason is "one cell" (the pooled value is the plain mean; also n by column), "no spread inside any cell" (every own weight is 1; also constant by column) or "no signal between cells" (tau2 is 0 and every own weight is 0; also sigma2 by column).

  • "spatialkit_pool_few_cells": 2 to 9 cells, so each target is the mean of all the other cells (cells, and own_weight, the smallest, by column).

  • "spatialkit_pool_few_df": sigma2 rests on fewer than 30 values beyond one per cell (needed, and df, n and cells by column).

  • "spatialkit_no_structure": structured is FALSE (see "Pooled values"). The text says which of the two tests failed, and beats is TRUE for a column whose pooled values beat one mean while the F test does not tell the cell means from one mean (also criterion = "loo", estimate = "pooled", and by column n, the cells, one_cell, loo and structure_p).

  • "spatialkit_pool_rows_skipped": rows with a value and a cell have empty or non-finite coordinates. They count in n and the plain columns and take no part in the pooled ones (n, cells).

  • "spatialkit_repeated_locations", with obs_level: rows with a value share a location. A residual leaves one row out and keeps the others at its location, so the interval then describes a further observation at a place already observed (n and total by column).

  • "spatialkit_few_residuals", with obs_level: fewer than five residuals are expected beyond each end of the interval, which at 0.90 is fewer than 100 residuals (needed, level, and n by column).

  • "spatialkit_estimate_mismatch" and "spatialkit_cells_differ": the two checks of the count record, described under "Value".

The two about few cells and few values are raised for columns whose weights were estimated, and the two of obs_level for columns whose interval is read from residuals, so a constant column raises "spatialkit_pool_degenerate" and no other.

References

Faes, C., Molenberghs, G., Aerts, M., Verbeke, G. and Kenward, M. G. (2009). The effective sample size and an alternative small-sample degrees-of-freedom method. The American Statistician, 63(4), 389–399. doi:10.1198/tast.2009.08196

Satterthwaite, F. E. (1946). An approximate distribution of estimates of variance components. Biometrics Bulletin, 2(6), 110–114. doi:10.2307/3002019

See also

assign_features_to_polygons(), which produces the input layer; build_tessellation() for the cells themselves.

Other aggregation: assign_features_to_polygons(), cell_values_at(), determine_optimal_levels(), kriging_adequacy(), resolution_profile(), select_resolution(), summary.resolution_profile()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
east  <- runif(n, 0, 100)
north <- runif(n, 0, 100)
# A response with spatial structure, so the within-cell ICC is not zero.
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + east, y = 5e6 + north,
             val = 5 + 0.02 * east + 0.02 * north + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
bnd <- st_sf(geometry = st_sfc(st_polygon(list(rbind(
  c(5e5, 5e6), c(5e5 + 100, 5e6), c(5e5 + 100, 5e6 + 100),
  c(5e5, 5e6 + 100), c(5e5, 5e6)
))), crs = 32632))
grid <- create_grid_polygons(bnd, target_cells = 9, type = "square")
assigned <- assign_features_to_polygons(pts, grid)

# Nine cells are too few for pooled values (each would be pulled toward
# all the other cells), so these summaries report plain means alone:
# estimate = "mean".
# IID standard errors (default) vs Kish design-effect adjustment.  The
# correction is large here, and meant to be: about 22 points per cell that
# all share the cell's part of the trend carry far fewer than 22
# independent pieces of information about the cell mean.
naive <- summarize_by_cell(assigned, response_var = "val", estimate = "mean")
kish  <- summarize_by_cell(assigned, response_var = "val", deff = "kish",
                           estimate = "mean")
data.frame(n = naive$n,
           se_naive = naive$..se_resp_val,
           se_kish  = kish$..se_resp_val)
#>    n   se_naive   se_kish
#> 1 25 0.09706775 0.7210227
#> 2 28 0.11815220 0.9279034
#> 3 25 0.11573069 0.8596517
#> 4 21 0.11556510 0.7881134
#> 5 23 0.13192931 0.9407000
#> 6 21 0.12707224 0.8665880
#> 7 10 0.18215988 0.8673238
#> 8 27 0.09534639 0.7355266
#> 9 20 0.14402822 0.9590654
attr(kish, "deff_applied")   # method, icc_resp, icc_pred, per-cell deff
#> $method
#> [1] "kish"
#> 
#> $icc_resp
#> [1] 0.6842466
#> 
#> $icc_pred
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 17.42192 19.47466 17.42192 14.68493 16.05343 14.68493  7.15822 18.79041
#> [9] 14.00069
#> 

# A 95% interval for each cell mean as an estimate of the grand mean, on
# the Kish-corrected standard error and n - 1 degrees of freedom.
ci <- summarize_by_cell(assigned, response_var = "val", deff = "kish",
                        conf_level = 0.95, estimate = "mean")
ci[, c("poly_id", "n", "resp_mean_val", "..neff_resp_val", "..df_resp_val",
       "..ci_lo_resp_val", "..ci_hi_resp_val")]
#> # A tibble: 9 × 7
#>   poly_id     n resp_mean_val ..neff_resp_val ..df_resp_val ..ci_lo_resp_val
#>     <int> <int>         <dbl>           <dbl>         <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1       1    25          5.63            1.43            24             4.14
#> 2       2    28          6.30            1.44            27             4.40
#> 3       3    25          6.93            1.43            24             5.16
#> 4       4    21          6.42            1.43            20             4.77
#> 5       5    23          7.11            1.43            22             5.15
#> 6       6    21          7.89            1.43            20             6.09
#> 7       7    10          7.16            1.40             9             5.19
#> 8       8    27          7.77            1.44            26             6.25
#> 9       9    20          8.16            1.43            19             6.15
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: ..ci_hi_resp_val <dbl>

# Pooled values, and a range for one observation: a smooth field plus
# noise at 400 points, on an 8 x 8 grid, so that a cell holds about six.
set.seed(2)
east  <- runif(400, 0, 8000)
north <- runif(400, 0, 8000)
pts2 <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + east, y = 5e6 + north,
             val = 10 + 3 * sin(east / 1500) + 3 * cos(north / 1200) +
               rnorm(400)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
bnd2 <- st_sf(geometry = st_sfc(st_polygon(list(rbind(
  c(5e5, 5e6), c(5e5 + 8000, 5e6), c(5e5 + 8000, 5e6 + 8000),
  c(5e5, 5e6 + 8000), c(5e5, 5e6)
))), crs = 32632))
grid2 <- create_grid_polygons(bnd2, target_cells = 64, type = "square")
assigned2 <- assign_features_to_polygons(pts2, grid2)
# estimate = "pooled" is the default.
pooled <- summarize_by_cell(assigned2, response_var = "val", obs_level = 0.90)
# The plain mean, the pooled value and the weight on the cell's own mean.
head(pooled[, c("poly_id", "n", "resp_mean_val", "..pooled_resp_val",
                "..pooled_w_resp_val")])
